guide.title: Steakhouses in Brooklyn: The Kosher Belt and Three Other Clusters
guide.intro: Fifteen rooms on this page, in four clusters that have almost nothing in common. Williamsburg and Greenpoint hold four, from the open fire at St. Anselm on Metropolitan Avenue to the binchotan charcoal at Salt + Charcoal on Grand Street. Five more make up a kosher steakhouse belt that runs from 40th Street in Borough Park through Avenue J in Midwood and East 7th Street in Gravesend to Kingston Avenue in Crown Heights. Bay Ridge and the Court Street corridor carry four, including two chop houses seven blocks apart on Third Avenue. Downtown Brooklyn has two. Peter Luger on Broadway and Gage & Tollner on Fulton Street are published on their own neighborhood guides and are named and linked here rather than repeated.

sections.heading: Williamsburg and Greenpoint
sections.body:
Four rooms in north Brooklyn, and each cooks its beef a different way.

St. Anselm on Metropolitan Avenue puts everything over an open fire, and the hanger steak is the order. It closed after an electrical fire in September 2024 and reopened in February 2025. DeStefano's is a few blocks north on Conselyea Street, a family steakhouse under pressed tin ceilings serving Prime dry-aged cuts. Salt + Charcoal on Grand Street is the Japanese room: binchotan charcoal on the robata, and A5 wagyu at the top of the menu. Amber, over the Greenpoint line on Nassau Avenue, calls itself the neighborhood's first steak house and runs from an eight-ounce filet up to a forty-eight-ounce porterhouse.

Peter Luger's brick corner at 178 Broadway and Driggs Avenue is a few minutes south of all of them. Its place page sits on the South Williamsburg guide, linked below.

sections.heading: The kosher steakhouse belt: Borough Park, Midwood and Crown Heights
sections.body:
This is the borough's second real cluster and the one nobody writes up. Five kosher steak rooms run in a rough line across the middle of Brooklyn, each closed Friday and Saturday for Shabbat, each built on grilled and broiled beef rather than on the deli menu the neighborhood is better known for.

The Loft is on 40th Street in Borough Park, with an upper loft above the dining room that takes up to seventy-five. Glatt A La Carte is on 18th Avenue, with sushi beside the steaks. Jerusalem Steakhouse has held its stretch of Avenue J in Midwood for close to thirty years, cooking prime kosher beef in an Israeli register. Mabat, on East 7th Street in Gravesend, is smaller and bring-your-own, with grilled meats and skewers off an open flame. MEAT, on Kingston Avenue in Crown Heights, is the newest of them, opened in 2019 by the team behind Basil.

If you are counting clusters rather than famous names, this one is the size of Williamsburg's.

sections.heading: Bay Ridge, Cobble Hill and Carroll Gardens
sections.body:
Third Avenue in Bay Ridge carries two chop houses seven blocks apart. Chadwick's at 88th Street is a Bay Ridge staple, an American room with an oak bar, high ceilings and a fireplace. Malone's at 95th Street, nearer the Belt Parkway, serves a dry-aged porterhouse and a dry-aged strip.

North along the Court Street corridor there are two more. Gus's Chop House on Union Street in Carroll Gardens is Chris McDade's room, drawing on the chop houses of Europe, and the Michelin guide lists it. Libertador on Henry Street in Cobble Hill is the borough's Argentine parrilla, opened in 2006 and built on gaucho-country cooking.

sections.heading: Downtown Brooklyn
sections.body:
Two rooms, both within a few minutes of the Fulton Mall. Peaches Prime is at 590 Fulton Street in the arts district by the Brooklyn Paramount, with aged steaks and simply cooked seafood at the heart of its menu. Fogo de Chão's churrascaria is inside City Point on Albee Square West, where the gaucho chefs work an open churrasco grill in the middle of the floor and carve picanha at the table.

Gage & Tollner is on the same street at 372 Fulton, a chop house that reopened in 2021 in its landmarked nineteenth-century room. It is published on the Downtown Brooklyn guide and linked below.

faq.question: What makes a room a steakhouse on this page?
faq.answer: Steak has to be the menu's center of gravity, plus the beef-centric genres — churrascaria, Argentine parrilla, Japanese wagyu counter, Korean-style beef room. That admits Salt + Charcoal's wagyu grill, Libertador's parrilla and Fogo de Chão's churrascaria alongside the chop houses. It excludes a bistro with a famous burger and a good steak on the card, which is a different kind of restaurant.

faq.question: Why are Peter Luger and Gage & Tollner not listed as rooms here?
faq.answer: Both already have place pages on their own neighborhood guides, Peter Luger on the South Williamsburg guide and Gage & Tollner on the Downtown Brooklyn guide. A room is published once in this site. This page names them where the geography calls for it and links to the guides that carry them.

faq.question: Is the kosher belt really a cluster, or just a list?
faq.answer: It is a cluster. Five rooms run in a rough line across Borough Park, Midwood, Gravesend and Crown Heights, they keep the same Sunday-to-Thursday week with the doors shut for Shabbat, and they are all built on grilled and broiled beef under kosher supervision. It is the same shape as the Williamsburg group and roughly the same size, and it is the finding that surprised this survey most.

faq.question: Which rooms did this survey check and leave out?
faq.answer: Hunter's Steak & Ale House on Fourth Avenue in Bay Ridge closed permanently in April 2026 after thirty years, and Embers on Third Avenue could not be confirmed as trading. Both were in the first count for Bay Ridge; neither is published, because a room whose door is shut is not a recommendation and a room whose status cannot be verified is not either.

faq.question: Where should a first visit go?
faq.answer: It depends what you want the beef to have touched. Live fire: St. Anselm on Metropolitan Avenue. Binchotan charcoal and wagyu: Salt + Charcoal on Grand Street. A dry-aged porterhouse in a plain old room: DeStefano's on Conselyea Street or Malone's on Third Avenue. A skewer carried to the table: Fogo de Chão at City Point.

photos.title: Peter Luger Steak House on Broadway at Driggs Avenue, Williamsburg, Brooklyn
photos.description: A four-storey red brick corner building on the wide intersection of Broadway and Driggs Avenue, its ground floor faced in dark green with gold Peter Luger lettering along the frontage. Traffic lights on a grey mast stand in front of it, a white minivan is parked at the kerb, a bus enters from the right and low brick row buildings run off to the left under an overcast sky.
photos.author: Leonard J. DeFrancisci

places.name: St. Anselm
places.summary: St. Anselm is a brick-walled room on Metropolitan Avenue in Williamsburg where beef, vegetables and seafood all go over an open fire. The hanger steak is the dish the room is known for.
places.history: An electrical fire closed the restaurant in September 2024 and it reopened in February 2025.

places.name: DeStefano's Steak House
places.summary: DeStefano's is a family-run steakhouse in a brick building on Conselyea Street, off the Graham Avenue side of Williamsburg, under pressed tin ceilings and beside a working fireplace. Prime dry-aged steaks are the menu.

places.name: Salt + Charcoal
places.summary: Salt + Charcoal is a Japanese robata room on Grand Street in Williamsburg where the beef is grilled over binchotan charcoal. A5 wagyu from Japan sits at the top of the menu.
places.history: Opened in 2014 by chef-owner Jiro Iida, and holds a Michelin Bib Gourmand for its robata menu.

places.name: Amber Steakhouse
places.summary: Amber is a steakhouse on Nassau Avenue in Greenpoint, which it describes as the neighborhood's first. The cuts run from an eight-ounce filet mignon up to a forty-eight-ounce porterhouse for two.

places.name: The Loft Steakhouse
places.summary: The Loft is a glatt kosher steakhouse on 40th Street in Borough Park, with an upper loft above the dining room that takes up to seventy-five. Ribeye, filet mignon and tomahawk carry the menu, and the doors close Friday and Saturday for Shabbat.

places.name: Glatt A La Carte
places.summary: Glatt A La Carte is a kosher steakhouse on 18th Avenue in Borough Park, open Sunday through Thursday and closed for Shabbat. Steaks anchor the menu, with sushi served alongside them.

places.name: Jerusalem Steakhouse
places.summary: Jerusalem Steakhouse has held its stretch of Avenue J in Midwood for close to thirty years. It grills prime kosher beef in an Israeli and Mediterranean register rather than broiling it in the American manner.

places.name: Mabat Steak House
places.summary: Mabat is a small kosher steakhouse on East 7th Street in Gravesend, certified by the Vaad Hakashrus of Flatbush. Grilled meats and skewers come off an open flame in Israeli portions, and the room is bring-your-own.

places.name: MEAT
places.summary: MEAT is a contemporary kosher steakhouse on Kingston Avenue in Crown Heights, opened in 2019 by the team behind Basil. The beef is under OU glatt certification and a creative Italian side of the menu runs beside it.
places.history: Closed during the pandemic and reopened afterwards on the same Kingston Avenue corner.

places.name: Chadwick's
places.summary: Chadwick's is a Bay Ridge steakhouse on Third Avenue near Fort Hamilton, a neighborhood staple with an oak bar, high ceilings and a fireplace. Steaks and chops carry the menu, with tiered seafood platters beside them.

places.name: Malone's Chop House
places.summary: Malone's is at the southern end of Third Avenue in Bay Ridge, near the Belt Parkway. A dry-aged porterhouse and a dry-aged strip steak carry the menu, in a room that reads as a neighborhood bar as much as a chop house.

places.name: Gus's Chop House
places.summary: Gus's is Chris McDade's chop house on Union Street in Carroll Gardens, drawing on the chop houses of Europe and on casual bistros. The chops run from leg of lamb to porterhouse and a dry-aged New York strip, and the Michelin guide lists the room.

places.name: Libertador
places.summary: Libertador is an Argentine parrilla on Henry Street in Cobble Hill, opened in 2006 and built on South American gaucho cooking. Beef grilled over coals is the menu.

places.name: Peaches Prime
places.summary: Peaches Prime is on Fulton Street in the Downtown Brooklyn arts district, a short walk from the Brooklyn Paramount. Aged steaks, simply cooked seafood and inventive plant-based plates are at the heart of the menu.

places.name: Fogo de Chão
places.summary: Fogo de Chão's Brooklyn churrascaria sits inside City Point on Albee Square West. Gaucho chefs work an open churrasco grill in the middle of the floor and carve picanha and the other cuts at the table.

entries.name: St. Anselm
entries.note: Metropolitan Avenue, Williamsburg. Everything crosses an open fire; the hanger steak is what the queue outside is for.

entries.name: DeStefano's Steak House
entries.note: Conselyea Street off Graham Avenue. Pressed tin, a working fireplace and Prime dry-aged beef, with none of the Williamsburg noise.

entries.name: Salt + Charcoal
entries.note: Grand Street, Williamsburg. The wagyu counter of this page: binchotan charcoal on the robata and A5 beef from Japan.

entries.name: Amber Steakhouse
entries.note: Nassau Avenue, Greenpoint. A forty-eight-ounce porterhouse for two at the top of the menu and an eight-ounce filet at the bottom.

entries.name: The Loft Steakhouse
entries.note: 40th Street, Borough Park. The upper loft takes up to seventy-five, which makes it the belt's room for a family occasion.

entries.name: Glatt A La Carte
entries.note: 18th Avenue, Borough Park. Steaks and sushi Sunday through Thursday; the doors close Friday for Shabbat.

entries.name: Jerusalem Steakhouse
entries.note: Avenue J, Midwood. The longest-standing room on the kosher belt and the one that grills rather than broils.

entries.name: Mabat Steak House
entries.note: East 7th Street, Gravesend. Small, bring-your-own, and the grilled meats and skewers come straight off the open flame.

entries.name: MEAT
entries.note: Kingston Avenue, Crown Heights. The eastern end of the kosher belt and the newest of its rooms, with an Italian side to the menu.

entries.name: Chadwick's
entries.note: Third Avenue at 88th Street. An oak bar and a fireplace, and a neighborhood room before it is a steak room.

entries.name: Malone's Chop House
entries.note: Third Avenue at 95th Street, seven blocks from Chadwick's. A dry-aged porterhouse and a dry-aged strip, near the Belt Parkway.

entries.name: Gus's Chop House
entries.note: Union Street, Carroll Gardens. Chops from leg of lamb to porterhouse, and a dry-aged New York strip beside them.

entries.name: Libertador
entries.note: Henry Street, Cobble Hill. Brooklyn's Argentine parrilla, and the one room on this page cooking beef over coals.

entries.name: Peaches Prime
entries.note: Fulton Street by the Brooklyn Paramount. Aged steaks and seafood, and the arts-district room to eat in before a show.

entries.name: Fogo de Chão
entries.note: City Point, Albee Square West. The churrasco grill is open to the floor, so the carving happens in front of the room.

links.note: Peter Luger's brick corner at 178 Broadway and Driggs Avenue is a South Williamsburg place, not a Williamsburg one, and its porterhouse is published on that guide.
Gage & Tollner at 372 Fulton Street, the chop house that reopened in 2021 in its landmarked room, is carried on the Downtown Brooklyn guide.
